Gary Mortimer, Queensland University of Technology/The Conversation It’s Saturday night and you’ve downloaded a new food delivery app. You’ve scanned the menus, picked some Mexican dishes, placed your order and are now tracking the delivery. But your food never comes – and you never expected it to. It sounds ridiculous if you’ve never tried it, but this viral trend is more popular than you might think. Just one app alone, FoodNeverComes, claims nearly one million “cravings satisfied” to date. Why would people bother spending time on apps or websites that are built to never deliver? Ultimately, it’s all about getting a dopamine hit. It sounds like harmless fun, letting users “buy” food, clothes or other products with no real-world cost, since most of these apps are free to use. But even when an app or website costs you nothing, there are downsides to watch out for – including how your choices can help advertisers better target you in real life. FoodNeverComes is one example of a free, ad-supported app and website that mimics an online food delivery service. But there are other types too. For instance, the free, ad-supported Dopamine Shop is a fake online shopping site. There, customers view items – everything from a 99-cent pet rock to a $99 million moon – then fill their carts. But no payment details are requested and no transaction ever occurs. Nothing is ever shipped. There are even fake, free “smoking” apps such as No Smoke Zone, also known as Virtual Smoke, which describes itself like this: Virtual Smoke is a realistic cigarette simulation app that lets you enjoy the look, feel, and relaxation of smoking – without any nicotine or harmful effects. Perfect for those trying to quit, reduce stress, or just have fun with a virtual cigarette. These new platforms are what’s known as “dopamine apps” or “dopamine sites”. While they began in South Korea, interestingly, Dopamine Shop is owned and developed by Fenwick Holdings LLC, a small independent studio in the US. This suggests this new genre of apps and websites may be spreading globally. Dopamine is both a powerful neurotransmitter and neuromodulator – delivering chemical messages and sparking changes in your brain. Dopamine plays several important roles, including motivating us toward goals and helping your brain learn which actions lead to beneficial outcomes. With these new dopamine platforms, users experience: The only element of the process missing, compared to a real app or website, is consumption (“I received it”). Even before these latest apps, some people had already realised they can get a similar retail therapy rush by creating wish lists or filling their cart, then deleting it, without making a purchase. You can simulate the same feeling by creating Pinterest boards of your dream home, without building a thing. Or you can imagine your dream holiday, using various free or paid travel planning apps and websites. Could pretending to order food, shopping or having “fun with a virtual cigarette” have any downsides? These dopamine apps and websites are relatively new, so we don’t yet have specific research on how much, if at all, they might serve as “gateway behaviors”. A gateway behavior is an initial behaviour that opens a pathway toward later behaviours becoming more likely. However, this is an area that’s been well studied before in other areas, such as gambling and gaming. And that past research raises potential concerns – particularly since these dopamine apps involve some level of gamification. For example, a notable 2014 study followed 409 people who played social casino games, but who had never gambled online with real money. Six months later, about 26% had migrated to real online gambling. A 2016 study of 521 social casino users found 19% reported gambling for real money as a direct result of social casino gaming. And a 2018 study of 1,178 German teens, aged 11 to 19, found that engagement with simulated gambling predicted subsequent real money gambling one year later. Remember the old saying, “there’s no such thing as a free lunch”? While these apps and websites might be fun and free, your fake choices can still be incredibly valuable for marketers. Free apps often rely on advertising to pay for making their content free. Apps or websites that use Google AdSense to display their ads use cookies: tiny text files stored on your browser to track your online browsing habits. Third-party advertisers, including Google, can then use your history to serve you more targeted ads. (If you read the fine print, sites note how to opt out of personalised advertising.) If you do purchase that pretend jacket, or order that delivery of fake tacos, don’t be surprised if you start seeing more ads for the real thing.Gary Mortimer, Professor of Marketing and Consumer Behaviour, Queensland University of Technology This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. "There are a lot of people who are able to play on PC"  I don't see Sony going back on their plans to embrace a discless PlayStation future, but I do wonder if they realised just how many of us would continue to talk about it for as long as we have. Even RPS got involved, and us PC lot had to abandon discs a millenia ago! And now Sega, former physical media producers themselves, have wandered into the conversation, even throwing a bone to the computer preferring collective that we all are.   Sega president Shuji Utsumi recently sat down in an interview with Famitsu (ta for the translations, GamesRadar), where he shared the company's stance on physical games. Here's what he had to say: "With regards to what we call 'full games' on both console and PC, we think the shift towards digital titles is key. Of course consoles are important, but at the moment, we're seeing an increase in the number of people playing on PC."   Utsumi goes on to acknowledge that there are regions that don't have easy access to consoles, noting that conversely "there are a lot of people who are able to play on PC. I think it's important to strengthen our digital products in order to develop this market. [Japan] has a culture of physical media, but I think it's necessary that we're conscious of digital content in order to become more global."   Where Sega ultimately stands is still in a place of being interested in physical games, especially considering their origins in that space. "We used to develop consoles, and of course, we still have a fondness for physical culture," he said. "So rather than completely abandoning it, we are currently considering the important elements of digital media, and simultaneously trying to make a shift."   The take away here for us is obviously Sega's interest in PC as a platform. Google spent years reforming Chromebooks to be seen as more than just laptops for schools that were destined for the e-waste bin. With the Googlebook, there might be more riding on this venture than you might think. For someone who has spent years exploring and enjoying the world of ChromeOS, the Googlebook announcement took me by surprise. Not only because Google is introducing something completely new, but also because of the path that led us to this point. I don't doubt Googlebook, I doubt Google Chromebooks got their start in 2010 with the Google Cr-48. It was never made available for purchase, with Google instead relying on a 60,000-person "pilot program." Fast-forward to June the following year, and Samsung released the first retail Chromebook, followed swiftly by Acer the next month. Back then, and for years to come, these early Chromebook models were really nothing more than Chrome-powered netbooks. Over time, Google got more partners on board, technology advanced, ChromeOS improved, and Chromebooks started arriving in a variety of sizes and designs. This was even true as Google released its own device, with the Chromebook Pixel arriving in 2013. Until then, Google left the hardware to manufacturers, focusing its resources on developing the platform. Google remained focused on improving ChromeOS, and, seeing the potential of expanding Android to more users, added the Play Store to ChromeOS in 2016. All the while, Chromebooks were never really marketed to the masses in the same way as phones or tablets. That's because Google didn't need to, as the education segment was (and still is) the bread and butter. According to one report, "Education accounts for 60.1% of the global Chromebook market share as of 2025." The same report also suggests that the Chromebook education market is "projected to hit $42.85 billion by 2034," up from $14.70 billion in 2025.  With Google making its money elsewhere, the build quality and the design of Chromebooks stagnated for years. That, compounded with the limited support cycles at the time, played major roles in the stigma of the platform still felt today. In 2023, Google seemingly realized the potential of Chromebooks for the non-education segment, but needed to improve its image. So in October, Chromebook Plus was announced. This aimed to take the pain and frustration out of picking between a bunch of bad apples, with the hopes of finding a gem. My Pixelbook is an elegant weapon for a less civilized age  Thanks to the world being rapidly taken over by an obsession with AI, so have our devices. It's practically impossible to do anything without seeing mention of Gemini, OpenAI, Claude, Grok, or just the phrase "AI." Given that ChromeOS is one of Google's software platforms, it was only a matter of time before Gemini was forced on everyone. It felt like Google was trying to push a square peg in a round hole, offering limited features that were hamstrung by the reliance on cloud computing. This would've made more sense in the earlier days of ChromeOS, as much of its functionality was tied to having an internet connection. However, as ChromeOS and Chromebooks have evolved, this is not so much the case, operating like a more traditional laptop, albeit one with modest specs (if I'm putting it nicely).  Because of the hardware limitations and need for the internet, it rendered Gemini essentially useless since AI models weren't stored on-device. While it was cool seeing Samsung's Galaxy Chromebook Plus arrive as the first with the dedicated "Quick Insert Key," it was useless when you were offline. In 2025, the "big break" came for AI on ChromeOS thanks to the arrival of the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14. Along with offering a premium design and up to 256GB of storage, the MediaTek Kompanio Ultra 910 chip made local, on-device AI processing, without an internet connection, more of a reality. The biggest Android release is right around the corner A few months after the debut of Lenovo's Chromebook, Google and Qualcomm not-so-subtly shared that something was coming. Now I know this is the Googlebook, but at the time, I wasn't really sure. Rumors and ramblings seemed to suggest that Google was working on a "Pixel Laptop," leaving some feeling like it was just a laptop with the same internals as an Android phone. Even as Google SVP for Platforms and Devices Rick Osterloh took the stage at the Snapdragon Summit with Qualcomm President and CEO Cristiano Amon, I was skeptical about what was to come. Google had already put in the work to make Android and ChromeOS more cohesive, so a new platform didn't make much sense. Nevertheless, that's exactly what we saw when the Googlebook was officially announced earlier this year. A new series of hardware and a software platform "designed for Gemini Intelligence." Complete with some callbacks to the early ChromeOS days, such as the RGB light bar on the top of the lid (hello, Chromebook Pixel). This is the part I think Google will struggle with. If you head over to the dedicated landing page and look through the provided imagery, there's nothing that tells me this isn't running ChromeOS. The desktop UI is the same, the app windows look the same, and even some (if not most) of the features are the same. Google clearly recognizes that, as the first FAQ tries to answer the question of what the difference is. Unfortunately, the answer doesn't do a great job of separating the two. So when it's released this fall, the Googlebook and Chromebooks will coexist, presumably until Google determines what to actually do.  I'm a big fan of Chromebooks and ChromeOS, especially with the strides made in recent years. However, I am a bit concerned about what the future holds, because I can't see both Chromebooks and Googlebooks living side by side for long. Likely, the Googlebook will be positioned as the "luxury" experience, while Chromebooks will continue to cater to those looking for more budget-friendly options. Curiously, there's no mention of Chromebook Plus here, but then again, it could just be Google being Google. Google remains committed to the ChromeOS platform, still offering 10 years of software support for newly released hardware. Perhaps Chromebooks will transition into being "Education-only" devices, as that's where most of the money remains. It also wouldn't come as a surprise if one day we wake up and see a new entry in the Google Graveyard. We want to hear from you. A pioneering facility has come online for its first season of low-carbon ammonia production in Minnesota, USA. The plant is being turned on gradually, with a target of one ton per day of low-carbon ammonia production for local fertiliser offtake. Wind energy powers the electrolysers that supply hydrogen to a Haber Bosch plant. To manage the fluctuating renewable energy supply, the rate of ammonia production can be adjusted using new modeling and control systems. The plant is located at University of Minnesotaâs (UMN) West Central Research and Outreach Center in Morris, rural Minnesota. It is a collaboration between UMN, Research Triangle Institutes International (RTI International) as well as Casale. The project aims to address high fertiliser prices and supply chain instability, while creating revenue streams within the state. This facility is an upscale of 2013âs successful pilot plant, and can be expanded further to a network of commercial, renewable ammonia generation hubs owned by farmer cooperatives. The ammonia produced can be stored in nurse tanks and/or coupled with carbon dioxide by-products from ethanol production to produce urea, the most common form of fertiliser used in Minnesota. It seemed like an elegant concept when we were first looking at it that you could take a wind turbine, and that’s producing energy from wind above a cornfield, or small grain field, and then produce a nutrient that you can use right underneath the wind farms in rural Minnesotaâ¦ There are no ammonia or nitrogen fertilizer production facilities in the state other than our small systems here. If you can produce a moderately priced nitrogen fertilizer that’s consistent, year in and year out, then farmers can budget for it, and they can market crops to that point in time. Michael Reese, Green Ammonia Research Lead, University of Minnesota Twin Cities press release, 26 Jun 2026 Essentially, the wind or the sun is our feedstock. We typically design a chemical plant to run at steady state and produce at a constant rate, assuming that we have a constant supply of our feedstock. That’s not the case with green chemicals or green ammonia specifically. In order to somehow absorb the fluctuations in wind availability, you need to have a significant storage of hydrogen to be able to absorb these fluctuations, which is very costly. On the other hand, if you allow the plant to operate dynamically, you minimize the demand for storing hydrogen or storing power and hence, you can have a much tighter design, a much, much more economical design. It’s about the economic development of the stateâ¦ One can see a model of co-ops that will come together and hopefully develop these plants with support and loans and credits from the state. Prodromos Daoutidis, Professor of Chemical Engineering, University of Minnesota Twin Cities press release, 26 Jun 2026 In AEAâs December 2025 episode of Project Features, project partners explained the Morris facility in detail among other ammonia energy R&D pioneering demonstration plants and start-up companies originating from the UMN. '80s kids know him as "Magnum, P.I." and '90s kids know him as Richard from "Friends." But who knows Tom Selleck as Jesse Stone? Well, your dad, probably. Selleck's "Jesse Stone" movies ran on CBS between 2005 and 2012 (a final film aired on the Hallmark Channel in 2015) and saw the veteran star play a police chief who he described to the A.V. Club as "a good man with some rather toxic habits." While the films typically appealed to older audiences, they're well worth watching for murder mystery fans. The movies are based on the "Jesse Stone" series of detective novels by Robert B. Parker, who's also the writer behind the book on which Ed Harris' criminally underrated Western "Appaloosa" was based. Parker authored nine Stone books prior to his 2010 death, after which several other authors continued the series. But Selleck is thus far the only actor to portray Stone on-screen. The character is a former LAPD detective who moves to a small New England town where he becomes police chief. While battling his own demons, Stone takes on the surprisingly corrupt forces that exist beneath the carapace of his ostensibly quiet hamlet. Selleck was inspired to bring Parker's novels to the small screen after his producing partner, Michael Brandman, gave him one of the books. As the actor told the A.V. Club, "I read it, and I said, 'I've got to play this guy!'" So, after the comforting purgatory of "Friends" came to an end in 2004, Selleck debuted as the detective in "Jesse Stone: Stone Cold," an adaptation of Parker's fourth Stone novel. It was the beginning of one of the actor's longest-running franchises. "Jesse Stone: Stone Cold" is set in the fictional town of Paradise, Massachusetts, where Tom Selleck's Stone is the police chief. Having been fired from the LAPD for his drinking problem before divorcing his wife and moving across the country, Stone is basically the jaded, grizzled detective archetype in action. But that's not a knock against the film or its sequels. Selleck is a perfect fit for Robert B. Parker's haunted cop. "Stone Cold" sees Stone investigate a series of killings in Paradise and a rape case while struggling with his drinking and womanizing issues. He's joined by a solid supporting cast that includes Viola Davis as Officer Molly Crane — a role she reprised in the next three films. Just to make things a little more confusing, "Stone Cold" is an adaptation of Parker's fourth novel, so the events of the film actually take place after the events of the 2006 follow-up, "Jesse Stone: Night Passage." Regardless, Variety's Brian Lowry seemed to like "Stone Cold," praising Selleck for bringing "an easygoing charm to this surprisingly well-crafted crime yarn." Lowry also wrote, "It's not much of a stretch to foresee it becoming a series of movies," which is, of course, exactly what happened. Over the course of eight more films, Stone investigates everything from a corrupt town council to organized crime and even a serial killer in Boston. He navigates an internal affairs investigation, explores cold cases, and negotiates hostage situations, all while taking stock of his own life. Surprisingly for a film series that only dads have ever heard of, a lot of the movies are actually great crime dramas, made all the more effective by Selleck's lead performance. Robert Harmon of "The Hitcher" fame directed all the films in the "Jesse Stone" series except for 2011's "Jesse Stone: Innocents Lost," which was overseen by Dick Lowry. Harmon went on to work with Tom Selleck on several episodes of his CBS procedural "Blue Bloods" and seems to have established a great working relationship with the actor, who began writing for the "Stone" film series as it went on. He and Harmon churned out "Jesse Stone" movies without compromising on quality, impressing author Robert B. Parker, who in a 2007 blog post wrote, "Tom nails the character." Sadly, following the broadcast of "Jesse Stone: Benefit of the Doubt" in 2012, Variety reported that the series was "over at CBS." Though the eighth film managed to pull in 13 million viewers the network was supposedly uninterested in its older demographic and was moving away from TV movies. At the time producer Michael Brandman described the cancellation of the film series as a surprise saying, "It's really hard for us to grasp." We did get one more film, however, after Hallmark financed a ninth installment: "Jesse Stone: Lost in Paradise." That was the last go round for Selleck's detective, though. In 2024, the actor spoke about the possibility of a final film, telling TVInsider "It looks like now I might have to write [a script for another movie.]. It wouldn't be a final one because everybody loves it [...] But I need to regroup; I don't know what's next." For now, we have the nine movies Selleck did make, which are scattered across the streaming sphere. You can see "Lost in Paradise" for free on YouTube, otherwise it's a case of renting or buying from the usual platforms.

The ELN wrapper embeds a call-selling exposure on the Nasdaq-100 while the underlying stock sleeve is an actively managed, defensive subset of the index. ByCourtney Connley-Hampton, Writer. Growing up in Detroit, Ryon Baldwin-Williams built web pages as a hobby. As a computer science major at Michigan State University’s School of Engineering, he got prized internships, working (among other stints) as a software analyst at consulting firm Accenture, and a software engineering intern at Rocket Companies, the big Detroit-based fintech built by billionaire Dan Gilbert. He even worked at MSU’s career services center during his sophomore to senior year, figuring it would help him network and learn about the resume tips, tricks, and skills needed to land a job after college. Yet more than a year after graduation, Baldwin-Williams, now 23, is still hunting for a permanent software engineering job. “I originally had a spreadsheet of every single job I applied to and the status of it,” he says. “But once I got to 100 applications, I said, ‘Uh-uh’ and deleted the whole thing.”  While lots of recent college graduates are being battered by a weak hiring market, perhaps no group is more shocked by their current plight than those who majored in engineering, long considered among the safest, most secure, and highest-paying majors. Yes, engineering grads still make more than education and English majors. The National Association of College and Employers projected in February that 2026 engineering  and computer science grads would see average starting salaries topping $81,000, compared to less than $69,000 for those majoring in business, social sciences and communications. But that’s if  they can find a job. In fact, the prospects for engineering grads are markedly worse than for other majors. According to LinkedIn data provided exclusively to Forbes, while overall hiring of new grads fell 20% between December 2019 and April 2026, jobs for engineering majors were down by 25%, the biggest drop for any of the 20 most common majors on LinkedIn’s platform. By contrast, jobs for education majors and those in the health professions slid 16%. “There was a time where we told everyone to code and we thought that was a very safe role,” says Kory Kantenga, LinkedIn’s Head of Economics, Americas. “And now we see for folks who graduate with computer science degrees, unemployment is relatively elevated.” Of course it’s not just new grads suffering. Outplacement consultant Challenger, Gray, and Christmas’ reports that in the first six months of this year, tech companies announced 139,156 jobs cuts, nearly one-third of all the layoffs announced by all industries. The dominant reason, the firm says, was artificial intelligence, “restructuring around it, automating roles, and reallocating budgets toward new [AI] capabilities.” But those layoffs hurt new grads too. As  fearful older workers cling to their current jobs, it has a cascading effect, meaning there are even fewer new openings for recent grads, says Kantenga. There’s another factor working against many engineers. In recent years, English, communications and performing arts majors have searched far afield to get their (admittedly lower paying) first jobs, with more than two thirds of grads from 2022 to 2024 working outside their core industries, according to LinkedIn’s analysis.  That’s a factor  it dubs “versatility.” But engineering grads, particularly those in certain subspecialties, stick to a narrower set of industries and paths. In today’s fast evolving job market, that lack of versatility has emerged as a growing handicap. The chart to the right shows the versatility score for different engineering specialties. Those who majored in aerospace and chemical engineering are facing the most challenges in today’s labor market–hiring in each specialty is off 26% and neither is particularly versatile. Civil engineers are faring better, Kantenga says, not only because construction is robust right now–there is, after all, a data center boom–but also because they have an underlying versatility. Yes, their versatility on the chart looks low, because they tend to stay in their core construction industry. But within construction, their versatility is actually high, he explains, because they can fill so many different roles–as project managers, project engineers and field engineers. Hiring of civil engineers, LinkedIn’s data shows, is off only 16% since December, 2019. Drilling even deeper into LinkedIn data, Kantenga reports that hiring for field engineers is actually up from pre-pandemic levels. “Field engineers are the people who support installing onsite equipment,” he notes. “So if you're graduating with a civil engineering degree and you go into field engineering, there's going to be all kinds of roles from everything related to transitioning to solar, to working at data centers.” The bottom line, says Kantenga, is that all engineering graduates need to hone in on where growth is happening in their field and figure out a way to tap into it. For example, he says, automation engineering, which includes designing systems that harness AI, is another area where hiring is up from pre-pandemic levels. He says engineering graduates now need to ask themselves, “How do I take the skills that I got from that major and apply them to another area or another field within engineering more broadly?”  As for computer software engineers, while hiring in their core industry is down 25%, they’ve got a versatility edge on say, chemical or aerospace engineers, since lots of companies need their skills. If AI means the tech companies aren’t hiring as many programmers, it also means that companies in other industries need tech specialists to help implement their own use of AI–and explain it to other employees. Provided that is, they have the communication skills to do so. The best engineering schools are (as engineers do) working on fixes. Consider the Georgia Institute of Technology, which has been honored on the New Ivies list of 10 public and 10 private schools employers love for all three years Forbes has published it.  Matthieu Bloch, associate dean for academic affairs and professor of electrical and computer engineering acknowledges the school’s engineering students are no longer getting “15 interviews and 15 job offers.” But they’re still doing relatively well, he says, because of its efforts to make their “students resilient to change.” In addition to creating an AI minor program in 2024 that spans the College of Engineering, College of Business, and College of Liberal Arts, Georgia Tech has focused on ensuring engineering students have the human soft skills needed to work in any field, Bloch says. And yes, it has actually harnessed AI to help students hone those skills. One of his colleagues, Bloch reports, has created AI-powered avatars for students to interact with. “These avatars represent different people depending on the context,” he explains. “They could be somebody who's a VC and the student has to do an elevator pitch to the VC. The avatar could also be somebody who's taking them through a technical review of their product.” The goal, he says, is to “leverage these new technologies to make our students better engineers, not just technically, but better at all the things that matter when working in a team in the workforce.” Case Western Reserve University, a private research university in Cleveland, also made this year’s New Ivies list. Susan Hagness, dean of the University’s Engineering School, says it too has emphasized to students the importance of mastering transferable human skills that will be needed regardless of AI’s advancements.  “Our engineering students can pick up a wide variety of courses across the curriculum and they often do,’’ says Hagness. “Many engineering students will pick up courses in philosophy and other humanities areas. I think that helps them stand out because while AI literacy is increasingly essential, we know from our employers that they value human intelligence skills that AI simply can't replicate.” Hagness reports that 98% of all 2025 Case Western graduates who pursued permanent employment landed a full-time job within three months of graduation. When looking at engineering students specifically, 23% landed jobs with starting salaries exceeding $100,000, she says. In today’s slow hiring market, Hagness says many of Case Western’s students start their job search about 10 months before graduation and keep their options open to opportunities that may not be in the traditional field for their major. “We're teaching our students to think critically and to be creative and to solve problems,” she says. “And that's always been in high demand across all industry sectors, so our students have not only gone into engineering, but consulting, healthcare, and financial services.” And what about Detroit resident and MSU grad Baldwin-Williams? As he continues his search for a full-time tech job, he’s using his own eclectic interests and communication skills to build a freelance business helping fashion brands build websites and other applications.  “I had to find a way to pursue what I wanted,” he says, adding that he’s now known as “the tech guy” in local creative circles.

While prediction market companies in the US continue to face legal battles between state and federal authorities, Robinhood is reportedly considering expanding its services. The company behind the cryptocurrency and stock trading app, Robinhood, is reportedly discussing plans to expand its existing prediction markets offering with crypto exchange Crypto.com. According to a Friday Wall Street Journal report citing people familiar with the matter, Robinhood was in talks with Crypto.com to place yes-or-no event contracts supplied by the exchange. The trading company launched its prediction markets hub in March 2025, initially facilitated by Kalshi in order to comply with regulatory requirements from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and later using ForecastEx and Rotella.  The reported move came just days after Bernstein analysts raised the firm’s price target on Robinhood (HOOD) stock to $160 from $130 per share, based on the company’s outlook for prediction markets and tokenized equities. They predicted Robinhood’s revenue using prediction markets could reach $1.7 billion by 2028. While Bernstein said in April that volumes in prediction markets could reach $1 trillion by 2030, many of the platforms face ongoing legal challenges in the United States between state and federal authorities. The CFTC has claimed to have “exclusive jurisdiction” over the companies’ event contracts, while gaming authorities in many states have filed lawsuits attempting to block or restrict their activities. When Robinhood Chain first launched, its activity was dominated by speculative memecoin trading rather than the original reason it was built — tokenization.  However, the momentum has finally started to shift, less than two weeks later.  Real-world assets now carry an active market value of about $70 million, according to DefiLlama, a roughly fivefold jump from the low tens of millions of dollars, which was a small slice of the network at just 4%, while memecoins and stablecoins accounted for most of the activity. The tokenized equities for which the chain was designed are finally trading in larger sizes.  A tokenized GameStop share is doing $26.6 million in daily volume on the exchange, with Nvidia at $14 million and SpaceX at $6.4 million close behind. Twelve Robinhood-based tokenized stocks are now clearing more than $500,000 a day, with five above $1 million. In its earliest days, the chain's busiest market was CASHCAT, a memecoin built around Robinhood's abandoned original name. The company was briefly "CashCat" before its founders settled on Robinhood. The token, which Robinhood has no part in, spiked more than 1,700% after CEO Vlad Tenev followed its account, then fell. It is now down about 75% from its peak, while a number of real equities trades in its place. Total value locked has roughly tripled since mid-July to about $312 million, according to DefiLlama, and Robinhood Chain is now clearing more than $600 million in daily decentralized-exchange volume, putting it among the more active networks in crypto. Its transaction count has also drawn attention, with more than 138 million in 30 days, per Token Terminal. But the chain's most-traded tokens are still overwhelmingly memecoins.  On DEX Screener, the top of Robinhood Chain's trending list is filled with tokens like “Hoodrat,” “Vladhood” and “Swole Doge,” not the tokenized equities the network was built for, which trade on Uniswap but rank well down the volume rankings. The tokenized stocks generate roughly $55 million in daily volume, under a tenth of the chain's nearly $600 million in total DEX trading, the data shows. The rest is dominated by memecoins. Stablecoins remain the single largest presence on the chain, with a combined market value in the hundreds of millions of dollars, and memecoins, such as the Robinhood mascot-themed CASHCAT, that defined the chain's first weeks, are still active and heavily traded. The critique three weeks ago was that Robinhood had built expensive infrastructure and attracted only speculation, with little sign that the tokenized-stock business it pitched would materialize.  That business is now materializing, in the form of tens of millions of dollars in real-world assets and a dozen equities trading in real size. However, it remains small compared to the chain’s stablecoin and memecoin ecosystems, and it will need to keep growing to meet Robinhood’s original vision for tokenization. But as the data indicates, the tokenized stock activity is moving toward the pitch rather than away from it as the company builds towards bringing millions of its retail customers onchain. Pete’s Pirate Life is Peter McKinnon’s EDC label. It put its name on another CIVIVI folder. The Iron Tide is the simplest thing that partnership has produced yet. Forest green aluminum, a black stonewashed 14C28N blade, a button lock, a titanium clip. Amazon has it at $84.75. CIVIVI’s own store wants $99.70. Price:  $84.75 Where to Buy: Amazon Most CIVIVI releases land as light, thin, undercut-everyone folders. Iron Tide doesn’t. It weighs 3.66 ounces and carries 3.7mm of blade stock behind a 3.24 inch edge. That combination makes it feel like a work knife wearing a designer badge. Some buyers want exactly that. The rest will feel every gram.  ADD US ON GOOGLE Specs first. Blade length runs 3.24 inches, overall length 7.62 inches, closed length 4.37 inches. The steel is Sandvik 14C28N hardened to 57 to 59 HRC, flat ground, clip point, finished in black stonewash. Handle scales are machined aluminum in forest green. Sandvik’s 14C28N is a steel budget folders keep coming back to. It sharpens fast and resists rust better than D2. Edge retention isn’t its strength. For a blade that opens boxes and rides in a pocket, that tradeoff lands right. CIVIVI runs the same steel through the Over Yonder, Vexron, and Kitefin. Deployment comes two ways, flipper tab or thumb stud, riding on caged ceramic ball bearings. The clip is 6AL4V titanium. It’s set up for tip-up carry, and that quietly eats into CIVIVI’s margin on a sub $100 folder. Over Yonder, Yonder, and Mini Praxis ship with plain stainless clips instead. In the box: a storage pouch, a cleaning cloth, stickers. Small thing. Including one at all reads as deliberate on a knife built for attention. Button locks reshaped the sub $100 category faster than any steel upgrade did. Press. The blade swings free, and your fingers never cross the edge path. CIVIVI tuned a spring under the button for enough resistance against accidental opening, but still enough give for a fast release. Caged ceramic bearings handle the rest. Washer pivots need breaking in and oiling before they drop shut. A caged bearing pivot skips all that and stays fast. The flipper tab adds the detent tension that launches the blade. Thumb studs on a flipper are usually decoration, but CIVIVI machined these from stainless instead of trim. The stud stays the slower route. A working flipper needs a firm detent that closes it with authority. Iron Tide weighs 3.66 ounces. The Kitefin carries a near identical 3.22 inch blade at 2.78 ounces. The Vexron breaks the pattern at 3.78 ounces, so mass isn’t unheard of in this lineup. Blade stock explains most of it. CIVIVI lists 0.15 inches here, versus 0.09 on the Over Yonder and 0.12 on the Button Lock Elementum II. That makes the Iron Tide the thickest of the three by a wide margin. Aluminum takes the rest. Scales machined 0.52 inches thick run denser than micarta or G10, and the titanium clip adds its own fraction. None of this reads as a mistake. Thicker stock resists lateral load, the difference you feel twisting the blade against a staple. Weight is the receipt for that stiffness rather than a bonus feature. Pick your priority. Shave an ounce off and you’d land closer to the Kitefin or the Over Yonder, both cheaper. The heft here is a choice, not an oversight. Amazon’s listing calls hand orientation ambidextrous. CIVIVI’s spec sheet says tip-up, right carry. Both can’t be true of the clip. The spec sheet wins here. A titanium clip machined for the right scale isn’t relocating. Left handed carry still works, since neither the flipper tab nor the button lock cares which hand you use. Clip position is the sticking point. The Over Yonder and the Yonder both ship tip-up L/R clips instead. Anyone carrying left should know that before ordering. CIVIVI lists the Iron Tide at $99.70 on its own store. Amazon has the same C25011-2 at $84.75. Fifteen dollars is a real gap on a sub $100 folder, even with free shipping over $10. Stack it against its own family. Kitefin sits at $69.70, Vexron at $63.75, and Over Yonder at $62.90, all wearing the same 14C28N. That’s fifteen to twenty two dollars above its stablemates. Our roundup of CIVIVI knives that outperform their price tags shows how tight that shelf is. Amazon currently carries the forest green C25011-2 alongside CIVIVI’s own listing. Stock on new colorways moves fast. This knife has been on shelves only a few weeks. Treat the current price as the price. Buy it for load work. Thicker stock, aluminum scales, and a button lock let you put weight behind this knife without second-guessing the lockup. $84.75 for that would have looked like a typo three years ago. Skip it for dress pockets. Nearly a full ounce over the Kitefin isn’t something a deep carry clip hides. Left handed carriers should pass as well, at least until CIVIVI ships a reversible clip. Building a first serious EDC kit? Start cheaper. Our field guide to EDC knife brands that earn the hype maps who’s competing at this tier. Price:  $84.75 Where to Buy: Amazon Iron Tide isn’t the lightest CIVIVI. It isn’t the cheapest, and it doesn’t carry the fanciest steel. It’s the one you’d hand to somebody who plans to use it. A 135mm f/1.8 full frame autofocus lens for $690 undercuts every rival on the market by a wide margin, and until recently, a lens this fast at this focal length simply didn't exist at this price. For portrait and event shooters chasing that tight, wildly out-of-focus look, the math suddenly changes. Christopher Frost runs the new 7Artisans 135mm f/1.8 through an independent test on his 61-megapixel Sony a7CR, and the results land where you'd expect for the money. The lens comes in L-mount, Sony E-mount, and Nikon Z-mount. It's a big, metal, seriously tough optic, weighing just over a kilogram, which is lighter than Viltrox's competing model but heavier than Samyang's version. Frost points out a metallic mount with a USB-C port for firmware updates, basic weather sealing, and a smudge-proof front element. Nothing rattles when you turn it upside down, and the manual focus ring turns smoothly and responds well to the motor. The controls are mostly good, with a couple of quirks Frost flags. The aperture ring clicks at every third of a stop, but it's easy to knock it out of A mode down to f/16 by accident, and there's no switch to lock it. Two customizable buttons and an autofocus-manual switch round out the body. The bigger issue is autofocus accuracy, which misfocused about 15 percent of the time on his a7CR in single-shot mode. Continuous mode sped things up considerably but didn't fix the accuracy, so his advice is to fire a few frames and check your shots in critical situations. He also notes a firmware update could plausibly tidy this up later. Image quality is where the price starts to look like a genuine bargain. Wide open at f/1.8, the center shows very good sharpness and contrast, tightening to perfect by f/2.8. Frost's copy was slightly decentered, so one set of corners stayed a touch ghostly while the other side impressed, a reminder that many lenses leave the factory with some misalignment baked in. Distortion is negligible, vignetting is surprisingly light, and the 68 cm minimum focus distance gives strong magnification for a portrait lens. Close-up work is hazy wide open but snaps sharp by f/4. Bokeh runs smooth overall, though bright specular highlights can show outlining and busy substructure. Understanding what a lens like this fits helps set expectations before you spend. A 135mm f/1.8 sits tighter than the familiar 85mm, which changes how you work a scene: you back up, you shoot compressed, and you isolate a face against a background that melts into color. That focal length rewards deliberate shooting, headshots, ceremony moments from a distance, tight candids, rather than run-and-gun coverage where a miss costs you the shot. The decentering point Frost raises applies across the whole lens market, not just budget glass, and it's the reason serious buyers test a new copy against a flat target before committing. Pair a lens like this with a 24- or 33-megapixel body rather than a 61-megapixel one, and the accuracy and sharpness demands ease off considerably, which is exactly the crowd this optic serves best. Frost's verdict is measured. The pricier competitors deliver more consistent critical sharpness and faster, more reliable autofocus, but this lens still produces spectacular images at a price that makes it an easy recommendation for anyone on a budget. Watch the accuracy, check your frames, and a properly centered copy could outperform even the copy he tested. Watch Frost's full breakdown in the video above to see the corner tests, the bokeh samples, and how it holds up on APS-C. Alex Cooke is a Cleveland-based photographer and meteorologist. He teaches music and enjoys time with horses and his rescue dogs.

Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more. Jul 25, 2026 — 6:00 AM ET First impressions matter, and Google’s learned that the hard way with its Tensor chipsets. We’re weeks away from the introduction of the company’s sixth-generation custom SoC, and there appear to be more questions than answers. Our recent survey found that users are frustrated and wary of buying a Pixel 11 until it’s clear what the Tensor G6 can do. I’ve used every Tensor chipset, and my outlook is different from the voters in our poll. The road hasn’t been perfect, and market circumstances have boxed Google in with the upcoming Pixel 11, but it hasn’t been the disaster some make it out to be. Here’s where Google went wrong with Tensor, and what I hope happens in the (very) near future. Whenever I write positively about Tensor chipsets, I’m met with a fair amount of backlash. I usually try to ask a couple of questions, and digging a little deeper often reveals the people commenting are disgruntled Pixel 6 and 7 owners, and I get it. Like many others, I got sucked into the fanfare surrounding the Pixel 6. It felt like Google finally had a coherent vision for its smartphones, complete with a custom chipset that would get it across the finish line. Unfortunately, the reality was far from perfect. The first-generation Tensor constantly overheated, throttling performance and shortening battery life. Subsequent updates dialed it in slightly, and the Pixel 6 recovered, but it was a few months of pain before that happened. The Tensor G2 in the Pixel 7 series wasn’t much better. It took a bit more to get that chipset to overheat, but it still happened. The phone’s polished aluminum frame often got hot to the touch during use, and I wouldn’t care if battery life didn’t suffer again. Google was off to a poor start, and many buyers wrote off Pixels (and Tensors). I was impressed by the Pixel 8 Pro when it was released. It was the first Pixel phone I could remember that delivered the battery performance I expected from a flagship. The overheating wasn’t completely gone, as many users still complained of hotter Pixels, but it was significantly reduced. Tensors never benchmarked as well as their Snapdragon flagship equivalents, but that didn’t matter on the Pixel 8 Pro. The user experience was (and is) silky smooth, and Google’s software extras were enough to keep fans happy. I’ve had similarly pleasant experiences with both my Pixel 9 Pro XL and Pixel 10 Pro XL. Google improved its modems, and each Tensor generation has been better than the last. The current Tensor G5 has been excellent in my usage. Yes, I understand that it doesn’t deliver the same gaming performance as other flagships, but many make it seem like you can’t game on a Pixel. That isn’t true. Most AAA mobile games run smoothly on my Pixel 10 Pro XL, but I notice a bit of lag at max settings. Pixels aren’t meant for enthusiasts. I understand that’s frustrating to some, especially given the phones’ flagship prices. But Pixel buyers are much more satisfied than they used to be. And while we might sit here and read benchmarks that don’t quite stack up to the competition, the only thing I’ve heard from numerous casual Pixel users is how much they love that Quick Share now works seamlessly with Apple’s AirDrop. The user experience is solid, and that’s what Google aimed to accomplish with Tensor. Unfortunately, the market is shifting. Rising prices put Google in an awkward spot with the upcoming Pixel 11. I respect what the company is trying to do, but when you push your pricing right up against Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra, which offers many of the same AI capabilities and Android features, it becomes tougher to justify any gap in value based solely on a better user experience. Yes, I prefer Google’s Material 3 Expressive design, and Android 17 has been fantastic on my Pixel 10 Pro XL, but buyers shelling out close to $1,400 are right to ask for everything. Leaks suggest Google understands this and is aiming to make the Tensor G6 more powerful, but it’s hard to believe the company can successfully change course and please buyers in only one generation. I hope Google can, because I love the progress it’s made over the last few years. Pixels are genuinely enjoyable to use, even if they don’t exactly fit the mold for every buyer. But to be successful, Google will need to get the Tensor G6 just right out of the box. It hasn’t been an easy road for Google with its Tensor chipsets, and I don’t blame a single person who was burned by the company’s early efforts. However, I can only review what’s put in front of me. Pixels have legitimately gotten better, and it’s unfair to make Google pay for its sins forever. The Pixel 11 will have a lot to prove, especially if it comes in at a much higher price, but I’m overall pleased with what Google’s done with its chipsets. Thank you for being part of our community. Sending You to Google News in 3  © JLGutierrez / E+ via Getty Images Gold has preserved purchasing power over decades, even centuries. That makes it a logical reserve asset for institutions like central banks, whose investment horizons are effectively perpetual. Most retirees, however, don’t have the luxury of waiting decades for that inflation protection to consistently pay off. In the meantime, owning gold comes with several trade-offs. Prices can be highly volatile, particularly when speculative enthusiasm is rampant. Moreover, most gold ETFs structured as grantor trusts are taxed as collectibles. That means long-term gains may be taxed at a maximum federal rate of 28%, higher than the 20% maximum rate that applies to most long-term capital gains. On top of that, gold produces no income. Unless you’re willing to periodically sell shares or generate cash flow through strategies like covered calls, it doesn’t naturally support retirement withdrawals. If my goal were protecting purchasing power during retirement, I’d look elsewhere. Rather than commodities or equities, I’d favor a particular corner of the fixed-income market: Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS. Unlike traditional Treasury bonds, the principal value of a TIPS bond adjusts with changes in the Consumer Price Index (CPI). As principal rises with inflation, the bond’s coupon payments increase as well because they are calculated as a percentage of that inflation-adjusted principal. TIPS generally outperform when inflation turns out to be higher than investors expected. Personally, I think the era of consistently achieving 2% annual inflation is behind us, at least for the foreseeable future. While investors can purchase individual TIPS directly from the U.S. Treasury, I prefer using an exchange-traded fund. ETFs simplify diversification, eliminate the need to manage individual maturities, and provide regular income distributions. My preferred choice is the Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF (VTIP). VTIP tracks the Bloomberg U.S. 0-5 Year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities Index. The short-term focus is what makes this ETF particularly attractive. Many TIPS funds hold securities with much longer maturities. While those funds still provide inflation protection, they also become much more sensitive to interest-rate changes. That’s important because periods of rising inflation (like 2022) often prompt central banks to raise interest rates, and longer-duration bonds generally experience larger price declines when rates increase. VTIP largely avoids that problem with an average duration of just 2.3 years. The trade-off is that it won’t benefit as much if interest rates fall sharply, but it also limits the downside should rates move higher. As a portfolio of U.S. Treasury securities, credit quality is about as strong as it gets. Every holding carries the backing of the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. One figure that often confuses investors is the fund’s 30-day SEC yield, currently 1.86%. That number represents the real yield before inflation adjustments. Your actual return consists of both this real yield and the inflation adjustment applied to the underlying TIPS principal. Because future CPI readings are unknown, Vanguard cannot incorporate those adjustments into the quoted SEC yield. Generally speaking, if inflation accelerates, both the principal adjustments and the income generated by the fund should increase accordingly. The first reason is simple: risk. Vanguard assigns VTIP a risk rating of just 1 out of 5 based on its historical volatility. For retirees holding significant cash balances that steadily lose purchasing power to inflation, replacing part of that cash allocation with a short-duration TIPS fund can be a sensible alternative while maintaining a relatively conservative risk profile. The second advantage is tax efficiency. Although VTIP pays distributions quarterly rather than monthly, the income generated from U.S. Treasury securities is generally exempt from state and local income taxes. That can provide a meaningful benefit for investors living in higher-tax states such as California or New York. No investment perfectly hedges inflation over every time period. Gold certainly has its place, particularly over very long horizons. But for retirees who prioritize preserving purchasing power, generating income, and minimizing volatility, I think short-term TIPS represent a more practical solution. The memory crisis has finally caught up to PC shipments as component prices continue to rise.  When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.  I've been keeping an eye on global PC shipments as part of the ongoing RAM crisis for more than a year, and it seems that the component shortage has finally caught up with markets. Global PC shipments dropped 4% year-over-year in Q2 2026 according to a new study by Counterpoint Research. That drop resulted in roughly 65 million shipments for the quarter, ending a growth run that had held since Q1 2025. This report lines up with what IDC predicted a few weeks ago: that global PC shipments will decline by 11.3% for the full year. In the same report, IDC analysts also predict that Q4 shipments could fall by a whopping 20% year over year.      The culprit behind the drop in PC shipments is the same as the one driving tech prices up seemingly across the board: soaring DRAM and NAND prices, driven largely by the sudden glut of AI data centers around the world. PC manufacturers have basically had to choose between raising consumer prices and eating raised component costs, and most have chosen the former. It's no wonder that PC shipments have finally started to drop off. Counterpoint notes that commercial PC buyers are proving to be the most resilient, helped along by ongoing Windows 11 migration from Windows 10. Without this uptick in PC sales, the overall picture would likely look a lot worse.      ASUS has undeniably been producing some of the best Windows laptops around lately, and I'm not exactly surprised to see it's the only Windows PC maker that saw a rise in global shipments. It improved by 4% year-over-year in Q2 2026, as Lenovo, Dell, HP, and other brands fell by up to 9%. It's worth noting that Apple had the best quarter, seeing its MacBook shipments climb by an impressive 13%. The popularity of its budget MacBook Neo undoubtedly has something to do with that number.      Counterpoint expects component prices to remain elevated throughout the second half of 2026. That's bad news for anyone who's on the lookout for budget PCs, as there are bound to be more price increases as OEMs struggle to maintain margins. The memory shortage is no longer just a short-term supply problem. It has become a key factor changing the direction of the PC industry. As OEMs face higher component costs, the market will shift toward premium AI PCs, since their better performance and on-device AI features make higher prices easier to accept. My best advice for anyone holding out for a cheap Windows PC? Don't. Just don't. As I've explained in my previous RAM crisis coverage, relief on pricing isn't expected anytime soon ... at least not before the end of 2027. If your current PC doesn't seem like it's going to live through another couple of years of dutiful service, it might be best to buy sooner rather than later despite the inflated costs already hitting consumers. Once federal, state, and local taxes come out of a money market distribution, the headline yield can lose a third or more of its value depending on the investor’s bracket and zip code. Three ETFs approach that problem from different angles: Alpha Architect 1-3 Month Box ETF (NYSEARCA:BOXX), Janus Henderson AAA CLO ETF (NYSEARCA:JAAA), and iShares Treasury Floating Rate Bond ETF (NYSEARCA:TFLO). Each uses a different mechanism to deliver more after-tax income than a taxable money market fund. BOXX restructures the character of returns from ordinary income into capital gains. JAAA reaches slightly further out the credit curve for a spread pickup while staying in AAA-rated paper. TFLO holds Treasury floaters whose interest is exempt from state and local income tax. The Fed funds rate is now 3.75% after cuts in October and December of last year, so the window for locking in cash-like yields has narrowed, and the tax layer has become a bigger share of the total-return equation. Aimed at taxable investors in a high federal bracket is this fund. The strategy uses box-spread options on the S&P 500, combining long and short call and put positions to lock in a defined return that closely tracks short-term Treasury yields. Returns come through as price appreciation on the fund’s shares rather than monthly distributions of ordinary interest. Held for more than a year, gains are taxed at long-term capital gains rates, which top out at 20% federally versus 37% on ordinary income above $640,600 for single filers in 2026. BOXX offers a tax-efficient alternative to traditional money market funds for high-income investors. The strategy has tracked its intended benchmark. BOXX returned about 4% over the past year and about 2% year to date, in line with rolling T-bill returns. The fund’s expense ratio is 0.19%, and it carries roughly $13 billion in assets, enough scale to support tight bid-ask spreads. The tradeoffs matter. Because gains accrue as appreciation, holders who sell within a year owe short-term capital gains, which are taxed as ordinary income and nullify the strategy’s core advantage. The IRS has not issued specific guidance blessing the box-spread structure, so there is a small risk that the tax treatment could be challenged. For investors with a multi-year horizon and a taxable account, BOXX converts a 4% cash-equivalent yield into a lower-taxed return. A different route is taken by this fund. Instead of engineering the tax character of returns, it earns a higher pretax yield by owning AAA-rated collateralized loan obligation tranches. CLOs pool senior secured leveraged loans, and the AAA tranche sits at the top of the capital structure, absorbing losses only after junior tranches have been wiped out. The historical default rate on AAA CLO paper is effectively zero, which is why the fund can offer higher income than Treasury alternatives without meaningful credit risk. This fund carries a distribution yield of roughly 4.95% paid monthly, on a share price of $50.57. The portfolio holds 608 positions across major institutional CLO managers, with the largest single holding at just 1.04% of assets. The fund manages roughly $27 billion in net assets, making it the dominant vehicle in the AAA CLO ETF category. The expense ratio is 0.20%. JAAA’s scale and credit quality make it a core holding for income-seeking investors.  Distributions from JAAA are taxed as ordinary income. The advantage is roughly 90 basis points of extra yield over comparable Treasury products, which more than compensates for the modest additional credit exposure for most investors. The floating-rate structure of the underlying loans means duration risk is minimal, though a sharp widening in credit spreads could cause a short-term drawdown, as happened briefly in March 2020. Oriented toward residents of high-tax states is this fund. The fund holds 99.6% of its assets in U.S. Treasury floating-rate notes across eight distinct maturities, with the remainder in a Treasury cash sweep. Interest on those Treasuries is exempt from state and local income taxes under federal law, which can add anywhere from 50 to 130 basis points of effective yield for investors in California, New York, or New Jersey compared with a taxable money market fund holding commercial paper. TFLO offers a tax-advantaged cash management solution for high-tax-state investors. The floating-rate structure resets weekly against the 13-week T-bill auction rate, so the fund’s yield tracks short-term Treasury rates almost in real time. That is useful in a stable-to-rising-rate environment and less useful if the Fed cuts aggressively, because distributions will drop within weeks. The current distribution yield sits at 3.8%, and the fund posted about a 4% total return over the past year. Net assets are around $6.7 billion, and the expense ratio is 0.15%, the cheapest of the three. For an investor in a state with no income tax, the case for TFLO over a plain money market fund weakens considerably, since the federal treatment is identical. The three funds sort cleanly by tax situation and risk tolerance. BOXX makes the most sense for high-income earners in taxable accounts who can hold for more than a year and want the return character shifted to long-term capital gains. JAAA fits investors willing to accept AAA-rated credit exposure in exchange for a yield premium of close to 1% over Treasury alternatives, and works well in tax-deferred accounts where the ordinary-income treatment is neutralized. TFLO is the default choice for residents of California, New York, and other high-tax states who want Treasury-level safety and are willing to accept a lower headline yield in exchange for state and local exemption. An investor comparing these funds to a money market fund yielding around 4% gross should run the math after taxes rather than on the headline. In a top federal bracket with a state income tax of 6% or more, the ranking of these three against a standard prime money market fund often flips once withholding is accounted for. Sending You to Google News in 3  © Pixel-Shot / Shutterstock.com  The stock market has spent much of 2026 rewriting the record books. Artificial intelligence spending continues to climb, hyperscalers are expected to commit over $1 trillion to new data centers next year, electricity demand is reaching levels utilities have never planned for, and IPO valuations have returned to nosebleed territory. Even Washington is setting records, with U.S. debt-to-GDP surpassing peaks last seen during World War II. It is becoming the year of superlatives.  Yet history shows that when every trend reaches an extreme at the same time, investors should spend as much time thinking about risk as they do opportunity. The clearest sign of investor enthusiasm comes from data from Strategas Research Partners and Bloomberg, which shows U.S. equity exchange-traded funds have attracted $880 billion of net inflows so far in 2026 — or more than every full-year total except the record set in 2025. Even more striking, inflows are running more than twice the pace seen at this point in both 2021 and 2025. If the current trend continues, investors will pour more than $1.4 trillion into U.S. equity ETFs this year — roughly $500 billion above last year’s record of approximately $920 billion. Those aren’t just healthy inflows. They’re unprecedented. The surge reflects investors’ confidence that AI investment, corporate earnings, and economic growth can continue supporting higher stock prices. Given the scale of spending announced by companies including Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG), and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), that optimism isn’t difficult to understand. Granted, strong inflows don’t automatically signal a market top. Bull markets often attract more buyers as confidence grows. The problem is that record optimism usually leaves less cash on the sidelines to cushion markets when sentiment changes. Investor enthusiasm isn’t showing up only in ETF purchases. FINRA data shows margin debt has climbed to a record $1.5 trillion, meaning investors are borrowing more money than ever to buy stocks. Leverage is a powerful accelerator. Rising markets magnify gains because borrowed money increases purchasing power. Conversely, falling markets can trigger margin calls that force investors to sell into already declining prices, creating a self-reinforcing cycle. Ironically, another corner of the market is already showing signs of stress. According to Reuters and LSEG Lipper data, U.S. investment-grade bond funds and ETFs suffered a record $7.1 billion in weekly withdrawals for the week ended July 22 after an inflation scare pushed Treasury yields higher. That shift highlights how quickly investor positioning can change when inflation expectations or interest rates move unexpectedly. None of this means a crash is inevitable. Corporate profits remain healthy, AI investment continues expanding, and many technology leaders are generating enormous cash flows that justify continued spending. Those fundamentals are real. That said, markets rarely move in a straight line forever. Today’s combination of record ETF inflows, record leveraged ETF buying, record margin debt, record AI capital spending, record data center construction, record electricity demand, record IPO valuations, and record federal debt creates a market with very little room for disappointment. Whether the catalyst is sticky inflation, higher interest rates, slowing earnings growth, geopolitical tensions, or an unexpected economic shock, markets that become crowded on one side can reverse faster than many investors expect. In short, the numbers tell a simple story: investors — domestic and foreign — have embraced U.S. stocks with unprecedented conviction. That confidence has been rewarded so far, but it has also pushed positioning to historical extremes. Smart investors don’t need to abandon the market simply because optimism is high. They should, however, recognize that record inflows and record leverage often amplify both gains and losses. Ultimately, the best defense isn’t predicting the next correction—it’s building a diversified portfolio, avoiding excessive borrowing, and keeping enough liquidity to take advantage of opportunities when others are forced to sell. Disney threatening to swallow its own tail isn't anything new. Long before the Mouse House struck box office gold with a string of live-action remakes of its own animated movies in the 2010s, the studio spent the 1990s rebooting older non-animated titles from its library. It wasn't all bad, mind you, as many people feel Nancy Meyers' 1998 screwball-flavored "The Parent Trap" (a redo of Disney's 1961 film adaptation of the novel "Lisa and Lottie") is better than the movie that inspired it. However, something like 1997's "That Darn Cat" (another revamp of a '60s Disney flick based on a book) mostly came and went. Then there was "Flubber," which the Mouse House released in between those two movies. A re-working of the studio's well-liked 1961 sci-fi comedy "The Absent-Minded Professor" (itself based on Samuel W. Taylor's short story "A Situation of Gravity"), the film starred Robin Williams as one Philip Brainard, a wayward professor whose new invention might just save his financially-downtrodden college. His creation? Flubber, a green goo with incredible kinetic energy that can just as readily be applied to heavyset objects (such as bowling balls) or even humans (!) to make them bounce around like springy rubber as it can allow cars to fly. Also, the Flubber is sentient, but it's better not to dwell on the ethical implications of that, much less the mechanics. If you're waiting for me to tell you that "Flubber" is a good movie that's stood the test of time, well, I'm sorry to disappoint. But rather than merely dunk on the film like critics did in its day (see: its 24% critical score on Rotten Tomatoes), let's take a look at how it became a box office hit and remains a time capsule of '90s pop culture in general. The nostalgia cycle meant 1960s nostalgia was all the rage in the '90s, which explains why Disney suddenly flooded the market with remakes of that decade's movies at the time, "Flubber" among them. Aiding the cause, the studio released the film theatrically over the Thanksgiving holiday frame in 1997. There, it thrived as a family-friendly foil to the R-rated "Alien: Resurrection" and other movies targeting adults. (It helped that Disney had screwed over the picture's would-be competitor "Anastasia," too, but that's another story.) Besides Robin Williams, the "Flubber" cast included Marcia Gay Harden as Sara Jean Reynolds (the president of Brainard's college and his fiancée ... whom he keeps absent-mindedly standing up at the altar) and Christopher McDonald as Brainard's ex-partner turned rival Wilson Croft. Indeed, there's no surer sign that you're watching a '90s flick than McDonald playing a total sleazeball (see also: "Thelma and Louise," "Happy Gilmore," etc.). And if that's not '90s enough, "Flubber" was written by John Hughes during the period where he was constantly repurposing the family comedy template that he himself established with his "Home Alone" script. Hence, "Flubber" goes heavy on the slapstick (even having someone expel Flubber from the wrong end) and gives McDonald's villain a pair of cartoonish goons played by the legendary Clancy Brown and Buffalo Bill from "The Silence of the Lambs," i.e. Ted Levine. Notably, "Flubber" was the second live-action remake that Hughes wrote for the Mouse House after 1996's "101 Dalmatians," another "Home Alone"-ish redux of a '60s Disney film (albeit this time an animated one). In both cases, critics found the results "pretty slow, flat, and dumb," to quote Roger Ebert's "Flubber" review. But commercially? These Disney remakes were quite profitable. The more things change...

When choosing a new Android phone for my personal use, I give most specs only a cursory examination. I can pick up any new     Android phone above $500, and its performance, battery life, and cameras will be more than sufficient for my needs.     However, the one element I regularly examine closely is the display technology. It's the only area of smartphone hardware that I continue to see notable developments in, which is why I'm fascinated by Samsung's new display technology and considering a Samsung foldable for the first time. Ignore the Ultra name The new Galaxy Z Fold 8 and its Ultra big brother feature a new display technology unimaginatively named Flex Titanium (because it uses a flexible titanium alloy). Samsung has been steadily improving its foldable displays since the first Galaxy Z device. It's easy to dismiss Flex Titanium as another marketing gimmick shrouding another step forward. But Flex Titanium isn't a step forward; it's a leap. As we found with our     hands-on of the Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra, the crease has almost completely disappeared.     This is the technology's most notable boon, but it doesn't stop there. The new display also brings anti-reflective improvements, which make the device a breeze to use outdoors for media (more on that soon). It boasts a peak brightness of 3,000 nits, a significant improvement over the Z Fold 7's 2,600 nits peak. The new display also allows more space for internal components, including a 4,800mAh battery. That's a 400mAh improvement over its predecessor. Charging speeds have also improved to 45W wired and 25W wireless, but I'm not sure this is thanks to Flex Titanium. To be worth upgrading, a device should boast improvements you don't need to look for. Performance upgrades are all well and good, but if they don't affect your phone in day-to-day use, do they really matter? A near-invisible crease. A uniform display. Anti-reflective properties. Peak brightness improvements. A bigger battery. These elements make a significant impact on using a foldable phone. Is Flex Titanium necessary for foldables? Technically, no. But it feels like it is. The other notable feature of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 (perhaps its defining feature) is its new aspect ratio. It's ditched long in favor of wide, and gosh, it's so much more satisfying to use. The aspect ratio of previous Z Fold devices was always a little awkward to use. But the black bars that plagued videos on the previous phone are lessened. Watching YouTube feels much more natural.  The benefits extend beyond videos. I read a lot of books on my phone, perhaps one a week. The experience is fine on my Google Pixel 10 Pro, but it would be stellar on the Z Fold 8 thanks to its book-style size. The strange thing is that this is mostly an illusion. Videos aren't any bigger on the Z Fold 8 than the Z Fold 8 Ultra (which retains the "old" aspect ratio). The black bars are just smaller. Reading is just as easy on a tall screen as a wide one. But the Z Fold 8 feels better. Sure, it's a little awkward to use one-handed, but isn't that every new phone? The Z Fold 8 isn't the first "wide" foldable. Huawei's Pura X Max, released earlier this year, boasted a similar design. The rumored iPhone foldable is also said to feature the same format. The Pixel Fold has featured a wider ratio in every iteration.     It's a clear shift in what manufacturers consider the "standard" for book-style foldables. The Z Fold 8 is the first foldable I've considered buying, but competition is about to get a lot stronger. It doesn't matter how good its design and features are; the Z Fold 8 Ultra's price starts at $2,100. $2,100. For a phone. If you're paying that much, you've missed out on one of the various deals currently available. For example, my carrier is offering the phone via a payment plan for a total of £1,476. That's a £500 saving. So in a year or so, when the second-hand refurbished devices start filling the market, and Black Friday deals add even bigger discounts, I'll finally be able to enjoy the Z Fold 8 for personal use. But until then, I'll     spend my money on fun and useful technology instead.     We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.
